overview: This file traces the Japanese silk industry’s deepening depression from April 1930 through June 1932 through State Department cross-reference sheets, economic-report excerpts, a consular despatch and newspaper enclosure, and a diplomatic telegram. It documents government-backed storage and bank lending intended to support raw-silk prices, contemporary press criticism of this intervention, experiments in cheaper cocoon preservation, restrictions on Japanese experts assisting Soviet sericulture, the industry’s mounting debts and bank exposure, and the controversial sale of more than 107,000 bales of government-held silk to Paolino Gerli through the Asahi Silk Corporation. Together the documents show how an agricultural export industry became a major financial and political problem for the Japanese government during the global depression.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report no. 42 on silk prices
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to report no. 42 concerning government action against the slump in Japan’s silk industry.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies a report from Castle dated April 7, 1930, filed elsewhere under political reporting. It summarizes the report as covering production curtailment, joint storage of raw silk, and Japanese government support for those measures.

subfiles.title: Report no. 42 excerpt on government silk-price support
subfiles.about: The report explains the Japanese government’s March 1930 measures to stabilize raw-silk prices and records press opposition to them.
subfiles.summary: With approximately two million households raising cocoons and raw-silk prices near their lowest level since 1921, sericulturists curtailed production and organized joint storage. The government guaranteed bank losses up to ¥30,000,000, subject to limits per bale, while the Imperial Silk Holding Company was to remove 50,000 bales from the market. The Tokyo Jiji and Tokyo Asahi criticized the policy as favoritism toward a poorly managed industry and as inconsistent with government retrenchment.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 54 transmitting a clipping on cocoon drying
subfiles.about: Garrels transmits a Japan Advertiser article about Professor Bunjiro Miake’s new cocoon-drying system.
subfiles.summary: The consul general forwards the complete information then available on a newly perfected cocoon-preservation method. The covering despatch reports Miake’s claim that the invention could save the silk industry at least $100,000,000 annually and states that no supplementary report is necessary.

subfiles.title: Japan Advertiser clipping on the Adozol Cooling System
subfiles.about: The clipping describes Bunjiro Miake’s experimental cooling system for preserving cocoons and its projected savings.
subfiles.summary: Miake’s Adozol Cooling System was being tested on twelve tons of cocoons at the Katakura company’s Ishiwara factory in Kumagaya, with final results expected the following February. The method cooled cocoons and continuously removed moisture instead of drying them with artificial heat. Its promoters claimed lower labor and operating costs, roughly 45 percent greater efficiency, reduced storage-space requirements, and as much as 20 percent more silk from a given quantity of cocoons.
keywords: Katakura Silk Reeling and Spinning Company

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 488 on silk experts and Russia
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a despatch reporting that Japan prevented silk experts from assisting Soviet sericulture.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies despatch no. 488 from Forbes and directs the reader to its location in another file. It states that the government feared Japanese silk-industry technical secrets would be lost if the experts went to Russia.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 488 excerpt on silk experts and gold shipments
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports government interference with Soviet contracts for Japanese silk experts and briefly discusses Japanese gold exports.
subfiles.summary: Six Japanese silk experts who had contracted to assist Soviet agriculture reportedly had to cancel their contracts under government pressure. The stated reason was fear that Japanese agricultural or sericultural secrets would be disclosed. A following section records ¥89,000,000 in gold shipments since the December 13 gold embargo and anticipates that shipments would soon cease.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram no. 107 on silk-industry finance
subfiles.about: The sheet points to section D of telegram no. 107 concerning the agricultural and credit structure of Japan’s silk industry.
subfiles.summary: The note emphasizes that silk production was primarily agricultural. It explains that filatures generally borrowed from banks to finance purchases of farmers’ cocoons rather than maintaining extensive deposits.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 107, section D, on silk-industry indebtedness
subfiles.about: The telegram estimates the Japanese silk industry’s debts, bank exposure, government liabilities, stored inventory, and depressed price level.
subfiles.summary: Neville explains that the capital invested in silk could not be measured accurately because production was dispersed among farmers and filatures dependent on short-term bank credit. The commercial attaché estimated outstanding costs above ¥250,000,000, including approximately ¥120,000,000 lent against more than 100,000 stored bales and perhaps ¥150,000,000 lent to some 3,800 filatures. Potential bank losses in liquidation were placed near ¥100,000,000, while the government owed banks ¥29,500,000 under the 1930 price-indemnification law. Current prices were about ¥650 per bale, against an estimated ¥800 needed for profitability.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornbeck memorandum on Japanese-American silk relations
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to a memorandum on the Japanese silk industry and its relationship with the American industry.
subfiles.summary: The underlying memorandum is filed under records relating to the Dai Ichi Raw Silk Corporation of America rather than reproduced here. The cross-reference identifies Hornbeck as its State Department author and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs as its recipient.
keywords: Dai Ichi Raw Silk Corporation of America

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 600 on the Gerli silk sale
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report that the Japanese government sold a large quantity of raw silk to Paolino Gerli through the Asahi Silk Corporation.
subfiles.summary: Although the OCR gives the year as 1952, the file chronology and associated report establish the date as May 2, 1932. The note identifies Gerli as president of the Silk Association of America and the Asahi Silk Corporation as his agent in the transaction.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 634 on complications from the Gerli sale
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a June report on complications resulting from the Japanese government’s sale of silk to Paolino Gerli.
subfiles.summary: The note records despatch no. 634 from Neville and directs researchers to the corresponding political report. Its subject is the continuing industry crisis created or aggravated by the government’s bulk silk sale.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 634 excerpt on the troubled aftermath of the Gerli sale
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes unresolved contractual and price-support problems following the sale of 107,850 bales of government silk.
subfiles.summary: The report says the bulk sale to Gerli had generated further complications instead of stabilizing the industry. Although the contract’s terms remained secret, one or both parties apparently had undertaken measures intended to sustain prices, but prices continued to fall. The new government therefore faced decisions about completing or cancelling the agreement, disposing of the silk after any cancellation, and preventing a further price decline.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 600 excerpt on the bulk sale of stored silk
subfiles.about: The excerpt reports the initial agreement to sell 107,830 bales of stored raw silk to Paolino Gerli through the Asahi Silk Corporation.
subfiles.summary: The report presents the transaction as the culmination of April discussions over the raw-silk crisis, while noting that the price, exchange rate, and payment method were still uncertain. It reports a price of ¥455 per bale and estimates a total loss of approximately ¥100,000,000, with the government liable for ¥30,000,000 and reelers and bankers bearing the remainder. The purpose was to liquidate silk accumulated during earlier attempts to arrest falling prices, which had continued to decline below the level prevailing before restoration of the gold embargo.

interest: The file is particularly useful because it follows a single commodity crisis from emergency price supports to mounting bank losses and eventual attempted liquidation of government-backed stocks. It juxtaposes official policy, Japanese newspaper criticism, diplomatic financial estimates, technological publicity, and anxiety over transferring sericultural expertise to the Soviet Union. The paired cross-reference sheets and excerpts also reveal State Department filing practices, while discrepancies between the reports—such as 107,830 versus 107,850 bales and the heavily corrupted forms of Paolino Gerli’s name—illustrate the evidentiary and OCR problems historians must resolve when reconstructing the transaction.
